title: Ezekiel 10:9–22
context: Ezekiel 10:9–22 describes the cherubim and the wheels, and the prophet twice identifies them with what he saw earlier: “This is the living creature that I saw by the river Chebar.” (10:15, 20; compare 10:22). The four wheels look like beryl, are like a wheel within a wheel, and do not turn as they go (10:9–11; compare 1:15–17). The cherubim’s bodies and the wheels are full of eyes all around (10:12), while 1:18 speaks of the wheels’ “rims full of eyes all around”. In 10:14 the first of the four faces is “the face of the cherub”, whereas 1:10 lists “the face of an ox”; readers offer various explanations, and these notes name the difference without harmonizing it. The glory then moves again: the LORD’s glory goes out from over the threshold and stands over the cherubim, and the cherubim mount up and stand at the door of the east gate of the LORD’s house, with the glory of the God of Israel over them (10:18–19). In chapter 11 the glory goes up from the middle of the city and stands on the mountain on the east side of the city (11:22–23), and much later Ezekiel sees it return by the way of the east gate (43:1–5). Both traditions read the departure of the glory as shared ground, holding that the LORD does not remain bound to a defiled sanctuary, yet the book holds out his return.

verses.text: I looked, and behold, there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one wheel beside one cherub, and another wheel beside another cherub. The appearance of the wheels was like a beryl stone.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel saw four wheels beside the cherubim, one beside each, with an appearance like beryl. Arminian readers note the echo of 1:15–16, named without harmonizing, and they see the vision of judgment drawing on the same imagery as the vision of the prophet’s call.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and observe that the identification of the stone rendered beryl is uncertain. They read the wheels as signs of the mobility of God’s throne, able to go in any direction, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: As for their appearance, the four of them had one likeness, like a wheel within a wheel.
verses.arminianNotes: The four wheels had one likeness, like a wheel within a wheel. Arminian readers note the repetition of 1:16, named without harmonizing, and they see in the image a picture of movement in every direction without turning, though the exact construction is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the precise picture loosely and read the image as conveying the freedom of God’s presence to move. They observe that the vision’s language strains to describe what it sees, and they do not try to reconstruct the wheels mechanically.

verses.text: When they went, they went in their four directions. They didn’t turn as they went, but to the place where the head looked they followed it. They didn’t turn as they went.
verses.arminianNotes: When they went, they went in their four directions without turning, following where the head looked. Arminian readers note that the movement is unified and purposeful, and they see the vision emphasizing that God’s presence moves according to his will rather than at random.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same unity of movement and compare 1:17, named without harmonizing. They read the description as conveying the coordinated purpose of the heavenly beings, a point both traditions treat as shared ground about the order of God’s presence.

verses.text: Their whole body, including their backs, their hands, their wings, and the wheels, were full of eyes all around, even the wheels that the four of them had.
verses.arminianNotes: The cherubim’s whole body, backs, hands, wings, and wheels were full of eyes all around. Arminian readers note that 1:18 speaks of the wheels’ “rims full of eyes all around”, and they name the difference in detail without harmonizing it, while seeing the eyes as suggesting all-seeing awareness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same difference and hold the symbolism of the eyes loosely, though many read them as suggesting God’s knowledge of all things. They observe that this fits the vision’s answer to the elders’ claim that the LORD does not see (8:12; 9:9).

verses.text: As for the wheels, they were called in my hearing, “the whirling wheels”.
verses.arminianNotes: The wheels were called in Ezekiel’s hearing “the whirling wheels”. Arminian readers note that the name emphasizes their rapid movement, and they see the vision’s language conveying the energy and power of God’s presence as it prepares to leave the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same name and observe that the term may also suggest a whirlwind. They read the verse as part of the prophet’s careful description, and both traditions see the naming of the wheels as adding to the vision’s sense of majesty and motion.

verses.text: Every one of them had four faces. The first face was the face of the cherub. The second face was the face of a man. The third face was the face of a lion. The fourth was the face of an eagle.
verses.arminianNotes: Each had four faces: the face of the cherub, a man, a lion, and an eagle. Arminian readers note that 1:10 lists “the face of an ox” where this verse has “the face of the cherub”, and they name the difference without harmonizing it, while holding explanations loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same difference and observe that various explanations have been offered, none of them settled. They read the four faces as conveying the fullness of creaturely excellence in God’s service, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: The cherubim mounted up. This is the living creature that I saw by the river Chebar.
verses.arminianNotes: The cherubim mounted up, and Ezekiel says, “This is the living creature that I saw by the river Chebar.” Arminian readers note that the prophet identifies the cherubim with the living creatures of chapter 1, and they see continuity between the vision of call and the vision of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same identification and read it as linking the God who appeared in exile with the God who now leaves the temple. They observe that the identification does not settle every difference in detail, and they name the parallels without harmonizing them.

verses.text: When the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them; and when the cherubim lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the wheels also didn’t turn from beside them.
verses.arminianNotes: When the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them, and when they lifted their wings to mount up, the wheels did not turn from beside them. Arminian readers note the unity of the cherubim and wheels, and they see the vision preparing for the departure of the glory from the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same unity and compare 1:19–21, named without harmonizing. They read the coordinated movement as showing that the whole vision moves under one purpose, and both traditions see it as preparing for the glory’s move to the east gate.

verses.text: When they stood, these stood. When they mounted up, these mounted up with them; for the spirit of the living creature was in them.
verses.arminianNotes: When they stood, the wheels stood; when they mounted up, the wheels mounted up, “for the spirit of the living creature was in them.” Arminian readers note the echo of 1:20–21, named without harmonizing, and they see one animating spirit directing the movement of the vision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and hold open how the spirit of the living creature should be understood. They read the verse as stressing that the wheels move not by themselves but by the life that directs them, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD’s glory went out from over the threshold of the house and stood over the cherubim.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s glory went out from over the threshold of the house and stood over the cherubim. Arminian readers note that the glory now leaves the threshold, the next stage of its departure, and they see God withdrawing from a sanctuary his people have defiled by their abominations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same stage, following 9:3 and 10:4, and read it as God’s righteous withdrawal. They observe that the movement continues to the east gate (10:19) and then to the mountain east of the city (11:22–23), and both traditions treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: The cherubim lifted up their wings and mounted up from the earth in my sight when they went out, with the wheels beside them. Then they stood at the door of the east gate of the LORD’s house; and the glory of the God of Israel was over them above.
verses.arminianNotes: The cherubim mounted up and stood at the door of the east gate of the LORD’s house, with the glory of the God of Israel over them. Arminian readers note that the glory pauses at the east gate, and they see in its gradual departure a God who leaves slowly, as though reluctant to go.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same pause and observe that the east gate is the place by which the glory will later return (43:1–5), named without harmonizing. They read the verse as a solemn stage in the glory’s departure, which both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: This is the living creature that I saw under the God of Israel by the river Chebar; and I knew that they were cherubim.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel says, “This is the living creature that I saw under the God of Israel by the river Chebar; and I knew that they were cherubim.” Arminian readers note that the prophet now names the living creatures of chapter 1 as cherubim, and they see his understanding growing through the vision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same identification and read it as connecting the throne vision of chapter 1 with the cherubim of the temple. They observe that the prophet’s knowledge comes by seeing what God shows him, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: Every one had four faces, and every one four wings. The likeness of the hands of a man was under their wings.
verses.arminianNotes: Each had four faces, four wings, and the likeness of a man’s hands under their wings. Arminian readers note that the description repeats details from chapter 1 (compare 1:6, 8), named without harmonizing, and they see the vision confirming the identity of what the prophet saw.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same repetition and read it as the prophet’s careful confirmation of the identification in 10:20. They observe that the detail of the hands recalls the cherub’s hand that gave fire to the man in linen (10:7), linking the description with the action.

verses.text: As for the likeness of their faces, they were the faces which I saw by the river Chebar, their appearances and themselves. They each went straight forward.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel says the faces were those he saw by the river Chebar, and they each went straight forward. Arminian readers note that the prophet again stresses continuity with the earlier vision, and they see the same God present in exile and in judgment on Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same continuity and observe that the prophet does not explain the difference noted in 10:14. They read the closing verse as confirming that the vision of judgment comes from the same God who called Ezekiel by the river Chebar.
